name: Central Serous Chorioretinopathy
preview_text: The quality of your blur - whether it feels like a fog, a wavy distortion, or a fixed dark spot - reveals which TCM pattern is driving the fluid under your retina, and each pattern...
synonyms: ["Central Retinal Disease", "Central Retinopathy", "Central Serous Retinopathy", "Central Vision Loss", "CSC", "Macular Retinopathy"]
conventional_description:
Central Serous Chorioretinopathy is a condition where fluid accumulates under the central retina (the macula), causing blurred or distorted central vision. It typically affects one eye and is most common in men between 30 and 50, often triggered by high stress or corticosteroid use. Diagnosis is confirmed with optical coherence tomography (OCT), which shows the pocket of fluid, and sometimes fluorescein angiography.
Many cases resolve on their own within a few months, but the fluid can return, and some people develop chronic or recurrent episodes that leave lasting visual distortion or thinning of the retina. The conventional view is that a leak in the choroid allows fluid to seep beneath the retina, though the exact reason for the leak is not always clear.
conventional_treatments: For acute CSC, doctors often recommend watchful waiting, as the fluid may reabsorb on its own. If it persists or recurs, treatment options include focal laser photocoagulation to seal the leak, or photodynamic therapy (PDT) to reduce abnormal choroidal vessels. In some cases, anti-VEGF injections are used off-label, though they are not FDA-approved for CSC. Oral medications like eplerenone or spironolactone, which affect mineralocorticoid receptors, are sometimes prescribed to reduce fluid, with mixed results.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands CSC primarily through the organ systems that nourish the eyes - especially the Liver, Kidney, and Spleen. The Liver opens into the eyes and stores Blood; the Kidneys store Essence, which rises to support clear vision. When these reserves run low, the retina can become undernourished and fluid balance falters. The Spleen transforms food into Qi and manages fluids; if it becomes weak or overwhelmed by dampness, turbid fluid can accumulate and drift upward, clouding the macula.
Fluid under the retina is seen as a form of Dampness, but the reason that Dampness forms varies widely. In one person, it may be because the Spleen is too weak to move fluids, creating a sticky, turbid dampness that fogs the vision. In another, it may be because Yin and Blood are so depleted that the eye tissues lose their integrity, allowing fluid to seep out. In still others, stagnant Blood blocks the tiny eye collaterals, causing fixed dark spots and wavy lines.
This is why two people with the same OCT scan can feel very different - one may feel heavy and sluggish, another dry and hot, and a third exhausted and washed out - and why TCM treats each differently.
The patterns also explain triggers. Stress, which is a major CSC trigger, directly disrupts Liver Qi flow, which can generate Heat or stagnation that rises to the eyes. Heavy, greasy meals can overwhelm the Spleen and generate turbid dampness. Late nights and overwork drain Yin and Qi, weakening the foundation that holds the retina steady. By tracing the fluid back to its source, TCM aims not just to clear the fluid but to correct the imbalance that allowed it to form in the first place.

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner starts by listening to how you describe your vision. Is it a gradual fog, a sudden distortion, or fixed dark spots? The quality and timing of the blur, together with your energy level, sleep, and digestion, offer the first clues. Tongue and pulse examination then confirms which pattern is driving the fluid under the retina.
When the main complaint is slow-onset blur with dry, gritty eyes and a feeling of heat in the palms or night sweats, the picture points to Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. The tongue is often red with little coating, and the pulse feels thin and rapid. This pattern shows the eyes are undernourished because the body’s cooling, moistening reserves have run low.
If the vision worsens after exertion and you feel deeply tired, short of breath, and washed out, Qi and Yin Deficiency is likely. The tongue may be pale or slightly red with a thin coat, and the pulse is weak or fine. Here the body lacks both the vital lift of Qi to send clear nourishment upward and the Yin fluids to keep the retina supple.
Fixed dark spots or wavy lines that do not shift, often with a prickly or distending sensation around the eye, suggest Blood Stagnation. The tongue looks dusky or has small purple spots, and the pulse feels choppy or wiry. Stagnation rarely stands alone; it frequently complicates a deficiency pattern, adding a layer of obstruction that traps fluid.
A heavy, cloudy veil across the vision with dizziness, a foggy head, and a greasy tongue coat points to Turbid Dampness obstructing the Middle Burner. The pulse is slippery. This pattern arises when digestion is sluggish, allowing dampness and phlegm to rise and mist the eye’s clear orifices, much like steam fogging a window.
When blurred vision comes with palpitations, restless sleep, poor appetite, and a pale tongue with a weak pulse, Heart and Spleen Deficiency is the root. The Spleen fails to make enough blood, so the Heart cannot house the mind and the eyes lose their nourishment. This pattern often appears in people who overthink or worry.

patterns.pattern_name: Turbid Dampness obstructing the Middle Burner
patterns.symptoms: ["Vision like looking through fog or a dirty window", "Heavy, wrapped sensation in the head", "Sticky or bland taste in the mouth, not thirsty", "Poor appetite and upper belly stuffiness after eating", "Loose, sticky stools and heavy limbs"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, rich, or fried foods, Dairy and cold raw foods, Damp, humid environments, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Warm, lightly spiced meals, Gentle movement or walking, Dry, crisp weather
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is overwhelmed by heavy, greasy foods or chronic dampness, it fails to transform fluids. A turbid, sticky dampness builds up in the middle burner and then drifts upward, clouding the clear orifices of the eyes. This misting of the visual pathway produces a sensation of fog or a veil over the vision, often with a heavy head and a sticky mouth taste.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with tooth marks; thick, white, greasy coating concentrated in the centre. Pulse: soggy (濡 ru) and moderate (缓 huan), or slippery (滑 hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness is a heavy, sticky pathogen that likes to settle and stagnate. Greasy, sweet, and cold foods add more dampness to the middle burner, directly feeding the pattern. Warm, aromatic foods and movement act like a gentle wind and sun, drying and dispersing the turbidity so it can no longer rise to cloud the eyes.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Warm, cooked meals with aromatic spices like ginger, cardamom, and a little pepper help the Spleen transform dampness. Reduce or avoid dairy, sugar, deep-fried foods, and raw cold salads, which all generate more turbid dampness. Gentle daily movement-like walking-keeps Qi and fluids moving so they do not stagnate.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver opens into the eyes and stores Blood, while the Kidneys store Essence that rises to nourish vision. When Liver and Kidney Yin run low, the eyes lose their deepest layer of moisture and nourishment. This leaves the retina dry and undernourished, causing gradual blurring and a sensation of something floating in front of the eye. The deficiency heat that often accompanies Yin depletion can disturb the delicate fluids of the macula, leading to the fluid leakage and central distortion typical of this condition.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, and wiry; weak in the left Chi (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin represents the body's cooling, moistening, and restorative energy. Late nights, overwork, and stress consume Yin, while heat and dryness further evaporate it. The eyes, as the sense organ most dependent on Yin for lubrication and clarity, are among the first to suffer. Rest, cooling environments, and moistening foods help preserve and rebuild Yin, allowing the eyes to regain their natural nourishment and visual sharpness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Go to bed by 11 p.m. to protect the Yin restorative window, and take frequent screen breaks to rest the eyes. Eat moistening, dark-colored foods like black sesame, goji berries, mulberries, and pears. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods, and keep alcohol and coffee modest. Gentle exercise like walking or Taiji supports Yin without overheating.

Excessive sweating or heat further depletes both Qi and Yin, deepening the deficiency and making central vision more blurry.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with fluid under the retina?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture works by improving local circulation around the eye and correcting the systemic imbalance that allowed the fluid to accumulate. Points around the eye like Jingming (BL-1) and Qiuhou (EX-HN-7) help drain fluid and bring fresh nourishment to the retina, while body points address the underlying pattern - whether that’s strengthening the Spleen, nourishing Yin, or moving stagnant Blood. Many patients notice their vision feels clearer and the distortion softens over a course of weekly sessions.

faqs.question: How long until I see improvement in my vision?
faqs.answer: Most people begin to notice subtle changes within 3 to 6 weeks of consistent herbal treatment and weekly acupuncture. The fluid itself may take longer to fully resolve on OCT - often 8 to 12 weeks - but visual symptoms like blur and distortion often start to ease before the fluid is completely gone. Deficiency patterns require more patience, as rebuilding Yin and Qi is a gradual process.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role and can make a real difference, especially if your pattern involves Dampness or Spleen weakness. In general, it helps to avoid greasy, fried, and heavily processed foods that create turbid dampness, and to eat warm, easily digested meals like soups and congees. Specific foods like goji berries, black sesame, and lightly cooked leafy greens are often recommended to nourish the eyes. Your practitioner will give you more targeted advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with my conventional eye treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be used safely alongside conventional monitoring and most treatments. If you are receiving laser therapy or photodynamic therapy, acupuncture and herbs can support healing and reduce the chance of recurrence. Always tell both your ophthalmologist and your TCM practitioner about all treatments you are receiving. If you are taking any blood-thinning medications, certain herbs like Dan Shen or Chuan Xiong may need to be avoided or adjusted - your herbalist will check for this.

faqs.question: What if my vision suddenly gets worse during treatment?
faqs.answer: Any sudden change in vision - such as a new curtain-like shadow, a shower of floaters, flashes of light, or a rapid drop in central vision - needs immediate evaluation by an eye doctor. This could indicate a different problem like retinal detachment. TCM treatment does not cause such events, but you should always prioritize an urgent eye exam if your symptoms change abruptly. See our Safety section for a full list of red-flag symptoms.

faqs.question: Will the fluid come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to reduce the likelihood of recurrence by addressing the underlying pattern that made you susceptible in the first place. Many patients who complete a full course of treatment - and maintain the dietary and lifestyle changes - find that episodes become less frequent or stop altogether. However, if the root imbalance is deep (for example, a constitutional Yin deficiency), you may need occasional maintenance treatments during periods of high stress or overwork to keep the eyes stable.

research.title: Effects of traditional Chinese medicine in the treatment of patients with central serous chorioretinopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This 2024 meta-analysis pooled data from multiple RCTs and found that Chinese herbal medicine significantly improved best-corrected visual acuity and reduced subretinal fluid compared to conventional treatment alone. The review highlighted moderate evidence quality and called for more rigorous trials.
research.periodical: Li J, et al. Effects of traditional Chinese medicine in the treatment of patients with central serous chorioretinopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine (Baltimore). 2024;103(26):e38594.

research.title: Treatment Of Central Serous Chorioretinopathy With Acupuncture, Moxibustion, And Chinese Herbal Medicine: A Case Report
research.description: This case report describes a patient with chronic CSC who achieved complete resolution of subretinal fluid and visual recovery after a combination of acupuncture, moxibustion, and a modified Chinese herbal formula. The treatment targeted Liver Qi stagnation, Spleen deficiency, and local blood stasis.
